This type of gourd, grown in Hit, Anbar Governorate, Iraq, is among a number of varieties of calabash or "bottle gourd" of different shapes and sizes that were historically used as multipurpose vessels, including water bottles and containers for agricultural produce including beer and wine, milk and other dairy products, honey or grains. Cut segments of these gourds could also be used to make kitchen utensils such as ladles and bowls. They have been cultivated in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas for thousands of years for similar purposes.
The double holes pierced near the top of some gourds enabled them to be tied together for transportation. These holes can later be plugged with sticks.

Both the Cairo aqueduct and Hama’s norias represent large-scale hydraulic infrastructure that brought river water into urban centres. While al-Nasir Muhammad’s aqueduct carried water from the Nile to the Citadel in Cairo, Hama’s wheels harnessed the river’s flow to lift and distribute it. Together, they show the ingenuity and variety of Islamic water distribution and management.

Large-scale water management relied on mechanical lifting systems adapted to different urban contexts. Monumental engineering supplied a fortified capital, while a locally venerated well sustained daily city life through a combination of technology, architecture, and belief.
Near Bethlehem, these Roman-era pools, later refurbished by Mamluks and Ottomans, channelled water by gravity to Jerusalem and local towns.

This dam in Algeria demonstrates how large-scale hydraulic structures were paired with local settlement and farming systems. Its flood-control and storage functions reflect a broader understanding of water as both a threat and a resource to be carefully measured, regulated, and shared in arid environments.

These reservoirs in Tunisia show how Islamic engineers combined technical skill and design to collect, filter and store water, complementing the broader story of urban water management and agriculture in the region.

Reflecting long traditions of capturing and preserving water in the region, this watercolour depicts the Spring House at Artas, a vaulted structure built into the eastern dam wall of the Lower Pool of Solomon’s Pools.

The *aflaj* irrigation systems of Oman are ancient water networks dating to around 500 AD. They use methods similar to Persian qanats, with underground tunnels and vertical access shafts. They combine water harvesting, storage, and distribution through surface channels, illustrating a continuous tradition of hydraulic ingenuity in the Middle East over 5000 years.

Bathhouse clogs were among the tools used during *hammam* rituals, protecting the body while it moved through wet spaces. Their presence alongside toiletry items emphasises how practices of cleanliness, bodily care, and social custom were carefully structured around water in domestic and ceremonial contexts.

Bathhouse textiles supported practices of cleanliness and modesty along with protective footwear. Together these objects show how the *hammam* was equipped with specialised items that structured bodily care and movement within wet spaces.

Perfume sprinklers were among the toiletry objects used in the hammam, where scented water accompanied washing and bodily care. Their use alongside mirrors, cosmetics, and clogs underscores how water, fragrance, and beauty practices were closely linked to ritual purity and social customs.

The arid environment and limited rainfall in the MENA (Middle East and North Africa) region made water an important source of charity, particularly at pilgrimage sites like the Haram al-Sharif. The establishment of Qaytbay’s *sabil* speaks to the universality of this public foundation and the importance of Jerusalem as a setting for Islamic patronage.

It documents the establishment and maintenance of the water supply serving the Haram al-Sharif, where access to water was essential for ritual purification and the daily functioning of al-Aqsa Mosque. The photograph captures a moment of continued care for the sacred complex within its historical and religious setting.

It is an example of a later and more monumental expression of the sabil tradition, emphasizing imperial patronage and public benefaction through water distribution. Together, they show how charitable fountains evolved architecturally while maintaining their core social and religious function.

It reflects the practice of offering free drinking water as a charitable public service. Elite patrons used sabils to support the community while expressing religious duty and civic presence in Ottoman cities.

Providing free drinking water functioned as both a social service and an expression of piety. Like the Sabil–Kuttab of Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda in Cairo, the fountain in Algiers demonstrates how elite patrons used water architecture to serve communities and assert their piety.

The engraving complements the sabil-kuttab by illustrating how water distribution and prayer spaces were visually and functionally linked, reinforcing the role of water in both charity and religious practice.

Water structures served to enliven architectural space and evoke paradisiacal imagery through pools and channels. Practical needs and symbolic meaning converged, demonstrating how water shaped both sacred experience and spatial aesthetics.

Flowing water enhances sensory experience by cooling space, producing sound, and providing comfort and contemplation. Decorative fountains transformed courtyards and gardens into refined environments shaped by movement and symbolism.

Water functioned as both a utilitarian element and a marker of luxury in palace architecture. Ornamental design and hydraulic purpose together reinforced the association among water, power, and elite space.

Cast in bronze in the form of a ram, this vessel functioned as a fountainhead or aquamanile in a palace or large residence. Water passed through its hollow body and flowed from the open mouth. Such animal-shaped vessels were popular across the Islamic world, blending symbolic imagery, craftsmanship, and the practical needs of domestic life.

Figural fountain elements shaped architectural spaces through flowing water and symbolic imagery. Such objects show how water features merged artistic experimentation with daily use in palace environments.

Zoomorphic fountain spouts transformed courtyards and gardens into dynamic sensory spaces through sound, movement, and ornament. Integrated into architectural settings, they reinforced the association between water, luxury, and paradisiacal display.

Monumental basins structured courtyard spaces by integrating water as a visual and symbolic focal point. Ornate decoration and scale reinforced associations among flowing water, luxury, and elite identity within palace architecture.

This well cover functioned as a protector of a courtyard well while ensuring controlled access to water. Both roles point to a shared architectural solution used in domestic spaces across al-Andalus and the Maghreb.

While the Seljuq ewer is a tool for the serving of liquids, the Fatimid strainer is a remnant of the preparation and filtering of water before use. Together they demonstrate the complete cycle of water use in domestic life — from purification to elegant presentation — and show how artistry infused even the most functional household tools.
Both the Seljuk and Blacas ewers highlight water-pouring as a refined art, but the Mosul example emphasises the cosmopolitan courtly culture of the AH 7th / AD 13th century.

The Mamluk ewer shows a continuity and elaboration of form, but with greater emphasis on heraldic and political imagery. All ewers in this series reveal how functional water vessels also projected power, prestige, and cultural identity across Islamic chronologies and geographies.

This illustration of al-Jazari’s water clock relates to the Midhat al-Sultan ablutions space through their shared role in structuring religious life in medieval Islamic society. While the ablutions room prepares the body for prayer through ritual washing, the water clock reflects the precise measurement of time within a culture organized around the daily rhythm of prayer. Together, they illustrate how water-based systems supported both bodily purification and the broader regulation of daily life in relation to worship.

While the Seljuq ewer is a tool for the serving of liquids, the Fatimid strainer is a remnant of the preparation and filtering of water before use. Together they demonstrate the complete cycle of water use in domestic life — from purification to elegant presentation — and show how artistry infused even the most functional household tools.

The *maada* model represents systems that regulated the fair distribution of water. It complements the use of water in everyday practice by illustrating how access to this resource was organised and controlled within communities.
Water infrastructure depicted on a banknote.

The *aflaj* irrigation systems of Oman are ancient water networks dating to around 500 AD. They use methods similar to Persian qanats, with underground tunnels and vertical access shafts. They combine water harvesting, storage, and distribution through surface channels, illustrating a continuous tradition of hydraulic ingenuity in the Middle East over 5000 years.

Noria al-Muhammadiyya is Hama’s most famous waterwheel and, together with the Ma’muriyya, one of its largest, with a 21 metre diameter and a long stretch of aqueduct still standing. It is one of the rare norias bearing an inscription.
